meeting_header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 15:00 - 15:46 UTC
Duration: 46 minutes
Location: Zoom
Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Monroe (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SA), Maya Lopez (CTO, CedarBay), Daniel Kim (Head of ML), Ravi Singh (Platform Eng), Sophie Tran (Security)
summary: Discovery call focused on Dedicated capacity: reserved GPUs, isolation (VPC/on-prem needs), burst strategy, autoscaling expectations, and security/compliance requirements. CedarBay is evaluating Dedicated to meet data residency and audit requirements; they run high-throughput inference for internal customer-facing agents and want predictable latency and cost. Redwood AE/SE outlined Dedicated offering, burst options, autoscaling, and next steps: pricing, SOC2 docs, and a benchmark run.
topics: Security: SOC2, KMS, SSO/SAML, audit logs
transcript: 00:00 Alex Monroe: hey everyone, thanks for joining. we're gonna run through dedicated capacity and answer Qs, i'm alex from redwood. priya's our se and liam will handle the bench stuff. 00:12 Maya Lopez: thanks alex, appreciate it. quick background — cedarbay is moving a lot of customer-support agents and internal risk scoring models to LLMs, need data isolation and predictable cost. 00:28 Daniel Kim: hi all, on the ml side we run real-time inference ~120 qps peak for the agent, typical request sizes around 300 tokens. latency needs are p90 < 400ms for text generation flows. 00:42 Priya Shah: got it, so you need low tail latency and isolation. just to confirm — is the data set PII-sensitive or regulated? 00:50 Maya Lopez: yes, some PII and payment tokens, so we need strict controls; procurement asked for SOC2 and network diagrams. 01:03 Alex Monroe: that's common; dedicated gives reserved gpus and a private tenant. we support private control plane (vpc peering or private link) and on-prem options if needed. 01:17 Ravi Singh: on the infra side we want to understand burst behavior — we have regular daily spikes up to 180 qps for short windows. how does dedicated handle bursts? 01:28 Priya Shah: we have a burst pool option — reserved baseline capacity plus burst buckets. baseline is guaranteed; burst is best-effort but you can configure fallback policies to a smaller hosted model or queue. latency for burst depends on circuiting and available GPUs. 01:44 Daniel Kim: is burst metered differently? we need cost predictability. 01:50 Alex Monroe: yes, burst is billed separately as a premium on top of reserved; we can show sample pricing tiers. also you can enable scheduled autoscale to add temporary reserved nodes if you can predict spikes. 02:08 Sophie Tran: from security — encryption at rest and in transit, we require customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) and full audit logs. does redwood support that? 02:18 Priya Shah: yes, we integrate with most KMS providers and can use customer-managed keys. audit logs, RBAC, and SAML SSO are available; i'll share the SOC2 and network diagram after this. small note — some product names get mangled in transcripts, but support is there. 02:36 Maya Lopez: great. another important thing: on inference optimization, do you support quantized models and mixed precision to lower costs? 02:45 Priya Shah: our runtime supports quantization-friendly execution, int8 variants, kernel selection optimizations and batching. we also have automatic prefix/KV cache which helps for chat workloads; that reduces token compute for repeated contexts. 03:02 Daniel Kim: can we pin model versions and force rollbacks if quality regresses? 03:08 Alex Monroe: yes, rollouts and canary by model version, plus automatic fallback to a previous variant. Redwood Console shows per-model perf and regressions tied to prompt evals. 03:20 Ravi Singh: network — we prefer private control plane with VPC peering. is inbound access needed from redwood, or is it customer-initiated peering? 03:30 Priya Shah: typically peering is set up from the customer's cloud account to ours; for private deployments we can do a customer-managed control plane where traffic never leaves the VPC. there are options for on-prem too. 03:45 Daniel Kim: regarding throughput — what's the expected tokens/sec per GPU for the models we discussed? we mentioned a mix of opens and newer encoder-decoder-ish models. 03:58 Liam O'Connor: ballpark for a 70B quantized to int8 on A100-ish hardware we typically get X tokens/sec in production, but that varies with sequence length and attention pattern — we'll run benchmarks. 04:12 Maya Lopez: can you be more specific on numbers? our finance team wants cost per 1M tokens. 04:18 Alex Monroe: we'll provide a pricing sheet with cost per token estimates by model and quantization. for budgeting we'll show reserved node hourly + token unit cost plus burst premiums. 04:33 Daniel Kim: ok, for sizing — we run ~120 qps baseline, burst 180, average tokens per call 300, concurrency about 40. what would you recommend? 04:46 Priya Shah: initial sizing candidate — 8 reserved GPUs to hit baseline with margin, plus a 2-GPU burst pool, but we should validate via a benchmark with your exact workload. 05:00 Ravi Singh: what's failover? if a dedicated region runs out, can we spill to hosted? 05:06 Alex Monroe: yes, smart routing can fail over to region or a hosted-compatible variant; fallback policies are configurable per-route. 05:18 Sophie Tran: audit trails — do you keep request-level logs? we need line items for GDPR/PII audit. 05:25 Priya Shah: we store audit logs and request metadata; full payload retention policies are configurable and can be set to zero-retention for sensitive calls. we'll include retention options in the security pack. 05:40 Maya Lopez: procurement question — what's typical contract term? monthly or annual? any commit discounts? 05:48 Alex Monroe: dedicated is usually reserved with monthly/annual commits; annual gives better discounts. burst and overage pricing are spelled out in the committed tier. 06:01 Daniel Kim: timeline — we want prod-ready in Q2 if possible. procurement and security review will take 4-6 weeks. can you support an accelerated PoC? 06:12 Alex Monroe: yes, we do 1-week benchmark PoCs frequently; we'll need access to a representative dataset (sanitized) and test harness. liam can run the bench and produce reports. 06:24 Liam O'Connor: i'll coordinate with ravi on the exact test harness. we'll measure p50/p90 latency, throughput, token cost, and failure modes. 06:33 Ravi Singh: we'll need an NDA and then a scp/transfer or s3 presigned for the dataset. 06:38 Alex Monroe: we'll send NDA and bench onboarding docs as next step. 06:43 Maya Lopez: any regulatory issues with cross-region data? we need EU residency for some customers. 06:50 Priya Shah: we run in multiple regions and offer region pinning; private deployment can be fully in-customer VPC for residency. 07:00 Daniel Kim: ok, some technical nit — how does KV cache invalidate across model updates? 07:06 Priya Shah: KV cache keyed to model version and session; when you update model version cache entries are invalidated unless you opt for compatibility mode. we'll include details in the bench docs. 07:20 Maya Lopez: are there limits on concurrency per tenant? 07:25 Alex Monroe: concurrency is function of GPUs and queueing policy; we can set per-route limits and the console surfaces token-level cost. 07:34 Ravi Singh: last thing — logging for debugging. we sometimes need traces for specific requests. do you expose tracing hooks? 07:41 Priya Shah: yes, tracing and per-request debug logs are available with redacted payloads as needed; we can provide access-scoped to your ops team. 07:55 Alex Monroe: cool, wrapping up — recap: we'll send pricing and contract template, SOC2 + network diagram, NDA + bench onboarding, schedule the benchmark week, and follow up with a meeting to review. 08:10 Maya Lopez: thanks — that sounds good. any immediate blockers from your side? 08:15 Daniel Kim: just need the bench to validate the 8 GPU recommendation; after that procurement will move to commit. 08:22 Alex Monroe: understood, we'll prioritize the docs and pricing. thanks everyone. 08:28 Meeting end
